steps.title: Number words
steps.intro: One word changes which numbers are allowed. Know every one exactly.

head: Word
Means
Examples
rows: whole number: negative, zero or positive
one number divided by another (denominator never 0)
same distance from zero, sum is 0
integers that differ by exactly 1 (consecutive even / odd: by 2)
what is left after whole groups; smaller than the divisor

tips: \(0\) is an integer, it is even, and it is neither positive nor negative.
\(1\) is not prime. \(2\) is the only even prime.
The opposite of \(x\) is \(-x\) — which is positive when \(x\) is negative.
The exam prints three of these in the general comments of every quantitative section: "0" is neither a positive nor a negative number. "0" is an even number. "1" is not a prime number.

steps.title: Exam words
steps.intro: The English words the exam uses for results and for kinds of numbers.

head: Word
Means
Example
rows: even (odd) numbers in a row: steps of \(2\)

tips: \(3\) is a divisor of \(12\) means the same as \(12\) is a multiple of \(3\).
The sum of the digits of \(507\) is \(5+0+7=12\), not \(507\).
A three-digit number cannot start with \(0\).

steps.stem: What is the sum of the digits of the smallest three-digit number whose digits are all distinct?
explanation: The smallest three-digit number is \(100\), but its digits are not distinct: it has two zeros.
Build the number from the left. The first digit cannot be \(0\): use \(1\). Then the smallest digits not used yet: \(0\), then \(2\). The number is \(102\).
The sum of its digits is \(1+0+2=3\).
Traps: \(1\) comes from \(100\) (digits not distinct). \(6\) comes from \(123\) (forgetting that \(0\) is a digit). \(102\) is the number, not the sum of its digits.

steps.stem: What is the product of the two smallest two-digit prime numbers?
explanation: The two-digit primes start \(11\), \(13\), \(17\), \(19\), ...
The two smallest are \(11\) and \(13\). Their product is \(11\cdot 13=110+33=143\).
The trap \(121=11\cdot 11\) uses the same prime twice. The question asks for two different primes.

steps.stem: Which statement about the number 1 is not correct?
choices: It is a divisor of every integer
explanation: \(1\) is odd: true. \(1\) is a natural number: true. \(1\) divides every integer: true.
But \(1\) is not prime. A prime has exactly two different divisors, and \(1\) has only one.
The false statement is choice 2.

steps.stem: m and n are opposite numbers. \(m + n = ?\)
explanation: Opposite numbers add up to zero. For example, \(m=9\) and \(n=-9\): \(9+(-9)=0\).
This is true for every pair of opposites. The answer is \(0\).

steps.stem: What will be the remainder if the smallest two-digit prime number is divided by 4?
explanation: The smallest two-digit prime is \(11\).
\(11=4\cdot 2+3\). The remainder is \(3\).

steps.stem: p and q are reciprocal numbers. \(p \cdot  q = ?\)
explanation: Reciprocal numbers multiply to one. For example, \(p=5\) and \(q=\frac{1}{5}\): \(5\cdot\frac{1}{5}=1\).
This is true for every pair of reciprocals. The answer is \(1\).

steps.stem: Which of the following numbers is a multiple of \(6\) and also a divisor of \(60\)?
explanation: A multiple of \(6\) is \(6\) times an integer: \(6\), \(12\), \(18\), ... A divisor of \(60\) divides \(60\) with no remainder.
\(12=6\cdot 2\) is a multiple of \(6\), and \(60\div 12=5\). Both conditions hold.
\(3\) is a divisor of \(6\), not a multiple of it. \(18\) is a multiple of \(6\), but \(60\div 18\) leaves a remainder of \(6\). \(120\) is a multiple of \(60\), not a divisor of it.

steps.stem: The sum of \(12\) and \(8\) is divided by the difference between \(12\) and \(8\). What is the result?
explanation: The quotient: \(20\div 4=5\).
Traps: \(\frac{1}{5}\) divides the other way (\(4\div 20\)). \(24\) is the product divided by the difference (\(96\div 4\)). \(80\) is the sum times the difference.

steps.stem: \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are three consecutive odd numbers, and \(a<b<c\). What is \(c-a\)?
explanation: Consecutive odd numbers go up by \(2\): for example \(7\), \(9\), \(11\).
Then \(c-a=11-7=4\). In general, \(b=a+2\) and \(c=a+4\). That gives \(c-a=4\).
The trap \(2\) comes from steps of \(1\) (\(7\), \(8\), \(9\)). But \(8\) is not odd.

steps.title: Must, could, cannot
steps.intro: Number-word questions ask which statement must, could or cannot be true.

head: Word
Means
How to answer
rows: find one example that breaks each wrong choice
true for at least one allowed number
examples that work knock out the wrong choices

tables.title: Numbers to test
head: Number
Why
rows: neither positive nor negative; anything times \(0\) is \(0\)
\(1\) is its own reciprocal; negatives flip signs

tips: Circle the word (must / could / cannot) before you read the choices.
Test only numbers the question allows: "positive integer" rules out \(0\), \(-1\) and \(\frac{1}{2}\).
Examples can kill a "must" choice, but only a reason proves one. When you have time, ask why the survivor always works.

steps.stem: \(x\) is a negative integer and \(y\) is a positive number. Which of the following must be true?
explanation: Plug in allowed numbers and try to break each choice. \(x\) is a negative integer. \(y\) can be any positive number, even a fraction.
Choice 1: \(x=-1\) and \(y=\frac{1}{2}\) give \(x\cdot y=-\frac{1}{2}\), not an integer. Out.
Choice 2: \(x=-1\) and \(y=5\) give \(x+y=4\), not negative. Out.
Choice 4: \(x=-1\) and \(y=\frac{1}{2}\) give \(x\cdot y=-\frac{1}{2}\), which is bigger than \(-1\). Out.
Choice 3 is always true: start at a negative number and subtract a positive one. You move further left of zero. For example, \(-1-5=-6\).

steps.stem: \(p\) is a prime number and \(q\) is an even number. Which of the following cannot be true?
explanation: For "cannot", one example that works knocks a choice out.
Choice 1: \(p=2\) and \(q=4\) give \(p+q=6\), even. Possible. Out.
Choice 3: \(q=0\) is allowed, because \(0\) is an even number. Then \(p\cdot q=0\). Possible. Out.
Choice 4: \(p=3\) and \(q=4\) give \(p-q=-1\), less than \(0\). Possible. Out.
Choice 2 is impossible: \(q\) is even, \(q=2k\) for an integer \(k\). Then \(p\cdot q=2\cdot(p\cdot k)\) is even, never odd.

steps.stem: \(n\) is a positive integer. Which of the following must be an even number?
explanation: Try \(n=1\) and \(n=2\) on each choice.
Choice 1: \(n=2\) gives \(3\), odd. Out. Choice 2: \(2n\) is even, and one more is odd, always. Out. Choice 4: \(n=1\) gives \(3\), odd. Out.
Choice 3: \(n\) and \(n+1\) are consecutive integers. Of two consecutive integers, one is even. A product with an even factor is even.
Check: \(n=1\) gives \(1\cdot 2=2\), and \(n=2\) gives \(2\cdot 3=6\).

steps.stem: \(x\) is a positive number. Which of the following could be true?
explanation: Test \(x=\frac{1}{2}\): \(x\cdot x=\frac{1}{2}\cdot\frac{1}{2}\) is half of a half, \(\frac{1}{4}\). And \(\frac{1}{4}<\frac{1}{2}\). Choice 2 could be true.
Choice 1: adding \(1\) always makes a number bigger. Never. Choice 3: \(x-x=0\), and \(0\) is not greater than \(0\). Never. Choice 4: \(2x=x+x\), and adding a positive \(x\) makes it bigger. Never.
With \(x=10\), choice 2 fails (\(100>10\)). That is why you test \(\frac{1}{2}\) too, not only whole numbers.

steps.stem: \(m\) and \(n\) are opposite numbers, and \(m\ne 0\). Which of the following must be true?
explanation: Opposites: \(n=-m\). Try \(m=3\), \(n=-3\) and also \(m=-3\), \(n=3\).
Choice 1: \(m=-3\), \(n=3\) gives \(m<n\). Out.
Choice 3: \(m=3\) gives \(3\cdot(-3)=-9\), not \(-1\). (Product \(1\) is the rule for reciprocals, not opposites.) Out.
Choice 4: \(m=3\) gives \(3-(-3)=6\). Out.
Choice 2: \(m\) and \(n\) are not zero and have different signs. Different signs give a negative product, every time.

steps.stem: \(p\) and \(q\) are reciprocal numbers. Which of the following cannot be true?
explanation: Reciprocals multiply to \(1\): \(p\cdot q=1\).
Choice 1: \(p=q=1\), and \(1\cdot 1=1\). Possible. Out. Choice 2: \(p=-2\), \(q=-\frac{1}{2}\). Possible. Out. Choice 4: \(p=2\), \(q=\frac{1}{2}\). Possible. Out.
Choice 3: if \(p=0\), then \(p\cdot q=0\) for every \(q\), never \(1\). Zero has no reciprocal.
Ones: \(3-6\) does not work. Borrow a ten: \(13-6=7\).
Tens: the \(9\) became \(8\), and \(8-4=4\). The answer is \(47\). Check: \(47+46=93\).
Adding a negative is subtracting: \(68+(-25)=68-25=43\).
The trap \(93\) comes from adding \(25\).
Ones: \(3-7\) does not work. Borrow a ten: \(13-7=6\).
Tens: the \(6\) became \(5\), and \(5-2=3\). The answer is \(36\). Check: \(36+27=63\).
Hundreds: \(8+1=9\). Thousands: \(4\). Total: \(4{,}929\).
Ones: borrow, \(13-7=6\).
Tens: the \(4\) became \(3\). Borrow again: \(13-4=9\).
Hundreds: the \(7\) became \(6\), and \(6-3=3\). The answer is \(396\). Check: \(396+347=743\).

steps.title: Signs and the times table
steps.intro: No calculator on the exam: the times table up to 10 × 10 must be automatic.
tips: Even number of negative factors → positive; odd → negative.
Anything times \(0\) is \(0\). \(0\) divided by a number is \(0\). Dividing by \(0\) is undefined.
Missing fact? Build it: \(12\cdot9=10\cdot9+2\cdot9=108\).
Last digit check: the last digit of a product comes only from the last digits. \(8\cdot 47\) ends in \(6\), because \(8\cdot 7=56\).
Estimate to knock out choices that are too big or too small: \(8\cdot 47\) is a little less than \(8\cdot 50=400\).

explanation: Different signs give a negative answer.
Sizes: \(63\div 9=7\). The answer is \(-7\).
Method 1 · last digit and estimate. The last digit comes only from \(3\cdot 7=21\). The answer ends in \(1\): choice 3 is out.
Estimate: \(23\cdot 47\) is more than \(20\cdot 47=940\). Choice 1 is too small. It is less than \(25\cdot 50=1{,}250\). Choice 4 is too big. Only choice 2 is left.
Check with the last digit: \(8\cdot 2=16\). The answer ends in \(6\), and \(458\) is out. \(38\cdot 12\) is less than \(40\cdot 12=480\), and \(546\) is out.

steps.title: Order of operations
steps.intro: Top to bottom, every time. Same level? Left to right.

head: Level
What
rows: Parentheses, brackets, and the whole top / whole bottom of a fraction bar
Multiply and divide — left to right
Add and subtract — left to right

tips: A minus before brackets flips every sign inside: \(5-(9-2)=5-9+2=-2\).
You may split a numerator, never a denominator: \(\frac{20+8}{4}=\frac{20}{4}+\frac{8}{4}\), but \(\frac{12}{2+4}\ne\frac{12}{2}+\frac{12}{4}\).

explanation: Multiplication comes before addition: \(6\cdot 5=30\). Then \(4+30=34\).
The trap \(50\) comes from adding first: \((4+6)\cdot 5=50\).
The fraction bar groups the whole bottom. Bottom first: \(3+6=9\).
The trap \(18\) comes from splitting the denominator: \(\frac{36}{3}+\frac{36}{6}=12+6=18\). That is not allowed.

steps.stem: Which of the following is equal to \(\frac{20+8}{4}\)?
explanation: A numerator may be split: every part of the top is divided by the whole bottom.
Parentheses first: \(2-5=-3\).
Then left to right: \(6\cdot(-3)=-18\), and \(-18\div(-3)=6\).
Inside the parentheses, division comes first: \(6\div 3=2\). The bracket is \(9-2=7\).
Or open the brackets. The minus in front flips every sign inside: \(5-9+2=-2\).
Method 2 · open the brackets. A minus before brackets flips every sign inside: \(20-8+3-6-4+9=14\).

Traps: \(2\) comes from flipping only the first number in each bracket (\(20-8-3+6-4-9\)). \(-4\) comes from forgetting to flip the \(-9\). \(4\) comes from \(20-11-5\): the two minus signs in \(-(-5)\) were not turned into a plus.
Or open the brackets and flip both signs: \(15-6+10=19\).
The trap \(-1\) comes from \(15-6-10\): only the \(6\) was flipped.
First bracket: \(12+(-7)=5\). Second bracket: \((-6)-(-6)=-6+6=0\).
The product is \(5\cdot 0=0\), and \(0-(-2)=0+2=2\).
Innermost parentheses first: \(7-4=3\).
Inside the square brackets, left to right: \(2\cdot 3=6\), then \(6\div 3=2\).
Finally \(24\div 2=12\).
Ones: \(4+8=12\). Write \(2\) and carry \(1\).
Ones: \(6\) is bigger than \(4\). Borrow a ten: \(14-6=8\).
Tens: the \(8\) became \(7\), and \(7-3=4\). The answer is \(48\). Check: \(48+36=84\).
A bigger number is subtracted from a smaller one. The answer is negative.
The difference is \(58-31=27\). Therefore \(31-58=-27\).
Two minus signs touching become a plus: \(73-(-46)=73+46=119\).
The trap \(27\) comes from \(73-46\): the sign flip was ignored.
Adding a negative number is the same as subtracting: \(95+(-38)=95-38=57\).
The trap \(133\) comes from adding \(38\) instead of subtracting it.
Both parts are negative. They pile up on the negative side of zero.
Add the sizes: \(62+25=87\). The answer is \(-87\).
We took away \(3\) too many. Add \(3\) back: \(504+3=507\).
Ones: \(8+5=13\). Write \(3\) and carry \(1\).
Tens: \(6+8+1=15\). Write \(5\) and carry \(1\).
Hundreds: \(4+1=5\). The sum is \(553\). Estimate: \(470+85\approx 555\).
Ones: \(6+5=11\). Write \(1\) and carry \(1\).
Tens: \(6+5+1=12\). Write \(2\) and carry \(1\).
Hundreds: \(6+5+1=12\). Write \(2\) and carry \(1\).
The last carry is the thousands digit \(1\). Total: \(1{,}221\).
\(994\) is \(6\) less than \(1{,}000\). Subtract \(1{,}000\), then give the \(6\) back.
Subtract in two pieces, \(606=600+6\).
Two minus signs touching become a plus: \(-3-(-11)=-3+11=8\).
Same signs give a positive answer.
Sizes: \(64\div 8=8\). The answer is \(8\).
From the times table: \(12\cdot 6=72\). Therefore \(72\div 12=6\).
Another way: \(12=3\cdot 4\). Divide in two steps: \(72\div 3=24\), then \(24\div 4=6\).
Split \(192\) into \(160+32\). Both parts divide by \(4\): \(160\div 4=40\) and \(32\div 4=8\).
Faster check: the last digit comes from \(9\cdot 3=27\). The answer ends in \(7\), and only \(117\) and \(97\) are left. Also \(9\cdot 13\) is more than \(9\cdot 12=108\). That rules out \(97\).

steps.stem: What are the quotient and the remainder when \(200\) is divided by \(6\)?
explanation: \(6\cdot 33=198\), and \(200-198=2\). The quotient is \(33\) and the remainder is \(2\).
Choice 3 is a trap: \(6\cdot 32+8=200\) is true, but \(8\) is bigger than \(6\). Another \(6\) still fits. The remainder must be smaller than the number you divide by.
Choice 4 is too big: \(6\cdot 34=204\), which is more than \(200\).
Parentheses first: \(5+2=7\).
Then the products: \(3\cdot 7=21\) and \(3\cdot 5=15\).
Last, subtract: \(21-15=6\).
Parentheses first: \(8-2=6\).
Then divide and multiply: \(18\div 6=3\) and \((-4)\cdot 3=-12\).
Divide and multiply first: \(12\div(-4)=-3\) and \((-6)\cdot(-2)=12\).
Then subtract: \(-3-12=-15\).
Brackets first: \(4-7=-3\) and \(-2-5=-7\).
Or open the brackets, flipping every sign inside: \(-4+7+2+5=10\).
The fraction bar groups the top and the bottom.
Top: \(5\cdot 8-4=40-4=36\). Bottom: multiply first, \(3\cdot 2=6\), then \(12-6=6\).
The value is \(36\div 6=6\).
The trap \(2\) comes from working the bottom left to right: \((12-3)\cdot 2=18\), and \(36\div 18=2\).

steps.stem: \(a\) and \(b\) are two consecutive integers. Which of the following must be true?
explanation: Test numbers that include zero and negatives.
Choice 2: \(a=0\), \(b=1\) gives \(a\cdot b=0\), not positive. Out. Choice 3: \(a=-2\), \(b=-1\) gives \(a+b=-3\). Out. Choice 4: \(a=8\), \(b=9\). Neither is prime. Out.
Choice 1: of two consecutive integers, one is even and one is odd. Even plus odd is odd. Check: \(0+1=1\), \(-2+(-1)=-3\), \(8+9=17\).

steps.stem: The product of two distinct positive integers is \(36\). Which of the following cannot be their sum?
explanation: List the pairs of positive integers with product \(36\): \(1\cdot 36\), \(2\cdot 18\), \(3\cdot 12\), \(4\cdot 9\), \(6\cdot 6\).
The two numbers must be distinct (different). The pair \(6\cdot 6\) is not allowed.

steps.stem: \(k\) is a positive integer. Which of the following cannot be a prime number?
explanation: Choice 1: \(k=1\) gives \(3\), a prime. Out. Choice 2: \(k=1\) gives \(2\), a prime (the only even prime). Out. Choice 4: \(k=1\) gives \(3\), a prime. Out.
Choice 3: \(6k=2\cdot 3\cdot k\) is at least \(6\) and divides by \(2\) and by \(3\). A prime has only two divisors, \(1\) and itself. Therefore \(6k\) is never prime.
The trap: many students cross out choice 2 as "always even". But \(2\cdot 1=2\) is prime.

steps.stem:
Given: \(-1<x<0\).
Which of the following is the largest?
explanation: Plug in a number in the range: \(x=-\frac{1}{2}\).
\(x=-\frac{1}{2}\). \(x\cdot x=\frac{1}{4}\) (negative times negative is positive, and half of a half is a quarter). \(-x=\frac{1}{2}\). \(\frac{1}{x}=-2\) (the reciprocal keeps the sign).
The largest is \(-x=\frac{1}{2}\).
Check another value, \(x=-\frac{1}{10}\): \(x\cdot x=\frac{1}{100}\) and \(-x=\frac{1}{10}\). \(-x\) is still the largest.

steps.title: Fast-calculation toolkit
tips: \(65^2\) means \(65\times 65\) (a number times itself).
Percent means out of a hundred: \(24\%\) of \(75\) is \(\frac{24\times 75}{100}\).

explanation: Add \(2\) to both numbers. The difference does not change.
That is two copies of \(37\) too many: \(3{,}700-74=3{,}626\).
Times \(9\) is times \(10\) minus one copy.
The trap \(854\) comes from subtracting \(6\) instead of \(86\).
Times \(11\) is times \(10\) plus one more copy.
\(25\) is a quarter of \(100\). Times \(25\) is times \(100\), divided by \(4\).
Times \(5\) is half of times \(10\): \(480\div 2=240\).
\(75\%\) is three quarters. A quarter of \(16\) is \(4\), and three quarters is \(3\times 4=12\).
\(39\) and \(41\) sit evenly around \(40\), with a gap of \(1\).
Front part \(8\), times the next number \(9\): \(8\times 9=72\). Then write \(25\) at the end: \(7{,}225\).
Cancel before you multiply.
The value is \(\frac{9\times 4}{2\times 3}=\frac{36}{6}=6\).

steps.stem: Which of the following is closest to \(\frac{398\times 51}{99}\)?
explanation: Round each number: \(398\approx 400\), \(51\approx 50\), \(99\approx 100\).
Each number moved only a little. The value stays close to \(200\) (the exact value is about \(205\)), far from \(150\) and \(250\).
